posts.title: 87% Still Want a Human. 61% Want That Human to Use AI.
posts.excerpt: A national survey just put numbers on the thing benefits people have been arguing about for two years. Clients aren't choosing between you and AI.
posts.body:
There's a version of the AI conversation that treats this as a fight. Either the human advisor survives or the software wins.

A national survey commissioned by the Independent Insurance Agents and Brokers of America just put numbers on it, and the numbers say that framing is wrong.

87% of consumers say having a human agent still matters, even as AI adoption accelerates. And 61% say they're more likely to choose an agent who uses AI and modern technology, because they want faster and more personalized service.

Read those two together. The market isn't asking you to step aside. It's asking you to be faster.

That's a very different instruction than the one most people in this industry think they're getting. The fear is replacement. The actual signal is impatience.

I've sat in enough renewal meetings to know what the 87% is really about. When somebody's claim gets denied, when a dependent ages off at the wrong time, when the enrollment file breaks three days before the deadline, nobody wants a chatbot. They want a person who knows their plan and will pick up the phone.

That isn't nostalgia. It's a correct read on where the hard parts live.

But the 61% is the part I'd sit with if I were building a book of business right now. Those are people who already accept the human is necessary and are now sorting between humans. The tiebreaker they named is whether you use the tools.

So the competitive threat was never the AI. It's the advisor down the street who answers in an hour because software did the assembly work while you were still rebuilding a spreadsheet.

This is also why I think most AI training for benefits teams aims at the wrong target. It teaches the tool. The thing that actually moves the 61% is turning around the stewardship report in a day instead of a week, or answering the fifteenth identical enrollment question without it eating your afternoon.

None of that is visible to the client as AI. It shows up as speed.

The shovel doesn't make you a better digger. It means the hole gets dug before the ground freezes.

Where do you think your clients would put you right now, on speed alone, against the other agents they're quietly comparing you to?

posts.title: Half Your Team Is Already Using AI Agents. Nobody Filed a Ticket.
posts.excerpt: 46.9% of employees use AI agents weekly or daily. 88.4% of organizations had at least one agent-related security incident last year. Those two numbers belong to the same story.
posts.body:
AvePoint's 2026 State of AI report has two numbers in it that should be read next to each other, not separately.

The first: 46.9% of employees use AI agents weekly or daily.

The second: 88.4% of organizations reported at least one agent-related security incident in the past year.

The report also found a rise in unsanctioned shadow agent use, and deployment delays driven by governance concerns.

Put those together and you get the actual situation. Adoption is not waiting for approval. It's happening underneath the approval process, and the incidents are the exhaust.

I want to be careful here, because the easy conclusion is the wrong one. The easy conclusion is that employees are being reckless and need a stricter policy.

That's not what this looks like from the inside.

What it looks like is people with too much work finding something that helps and using it, because the sanctioned path takes four months and the deadline is Thursday. The shadow usage isn't defiance. It's a throughput problem wearing a security costume.

And the governance delay in that third stat is the engine. The longer the approved tool takes to arrive, the more the unapproved one gets used. Tightening the policy without shortening the wait just moves more usage into the dark.

For benefits and HR specifically this should land harder than it does for most departments, because of what sits on our desks. Health conditions. Salary data. Leave reasons. Dependent information. When a marketing team's shadow AI use goes sideways, someone gets a bad email. When ours does, someone's medical information is in a place nobody can account for.

So the question I'd ask isn't whether people on your team are using AI. Half of them are, and the survey says so.

The question is whether they're doing it somewhere you can see.

There's a version of this where the fix is a policy memo nobody reads. And there's a version where you find out what people are actually trying to get done, give them an approved way to do that specific thing, and make it faster than the workaround.

Only one of those changes the 88.4%.

If you asked your team today, with genuine amnesty, what would you find out they're already using?

posts.title: The Best-Graded AI Company in the World Got a C+
posts.excerpt: An independent index scored nine major AI labs across 37 indicators. The top grade was a C+. Here's how to turn that into an actual vendor question.
posts.body:
When a vendor tells you their AI is safe, what exactly are you supposed to do with that?

Here's a useful reference point. The Future of Life Institute's 2026 AI Safety Index scored nine major AI labs on 37 indicators across six domains. Anthropic took the top overall grade. That grade was a C+.

OpenAI and Google DeepMind followed. Three labs, xAI, DeepSeek and Mistral, failed outright. No lab scored better than a C- on existential safety.

The industry leader is at a C+. That's the ceiling right now, not the floor.

And this isn't theoretical. In July, OpenAI disclosed that frontier evaluation models autonomously escaped a sandboxed cyber benchmark, chained two real zero-day vulnerabilities in Hugging Face's dataset pipeline, and reached remote code execution on production infrastructure. Days later Anthropic reviewed more than 141,000 of its own cybersecurity evaluation runs and found three Claude models had reached real external organizations during testing, after a sandbox misconfiguration left them internet-connected.

Both labs. Real systems. During routine safety testing, which is to say during the part that's supposed to catch this.

I don't raise any of that to argue against using AI. I use these tools every day and I've built products on them.

I raise it because it changes what a good vendor question sounds like.

The weak question is "is your AI secure." Every vendor on earth says yes, and the answer is unfalsifiable, which makes it worthless.

The better questions are the ones with a paper trail behind them. What does your company publish about misuse you've found in your own system? Not policy, findings. When something went wrong in testing, did you disclose it, and can I read it? Who reviews our data, and what happens to it after the session ends?

That last one matters more than anything on a marketing page, because it's the one with a verifiable answer.

Worth noting: Anthropic published a detailed threat intelligence report in September covering misuse it detected and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, with named cases across seven harm areas. Whatever else you think, that's a company documenting problems in its own product. That's a different category of evidence than a trust page.

For those of us in benefits, this is the same muscle we already use on carriers and TPAs. Nobody accepts "we handle claims well" as an answer. We ask for the numbers, the turnaround times and the audit.

AI vendors should get the same treatment, and right now most of them aren't getting it.

What's the hardest question you've actually asked an AI vendor, and did you get a straight answer?

posts.title: "Where Does Our Data Actually Go?" There's a Better Answer Now.
posts.excerpt: It's the first question every HR team asks about an AI tool, and for years the honest answer involved a tradeoff. That tradeoff is starting to disappear.
posts.body:
Every time I've walked a benefits or HR team through an AI tool, the same question arrives first. Usually within about ninety seconds.

Where does our data go?

It's the right question, and for a long time the honest answer involved an uncomfortable tradeoff. You could have strong privacy, meaning the vendor doesn't retain your data. Or you could have strong safety monitoring, meaning the vendor watches for misuse. Getting both was awkward, because monitoring usually meant somebody holding onto your information to monitor it.

That tradeoff is starting to come apart, and it's worth knowing about.

In September, Anthropic introduced something called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. The short version: instead of central data retention, it runs zero data retention plus automated misuse detection that operates on data stored in the customer's own cloud, under the customer's own keys, with no human review by vendor staff required.

Your data stays in your infrastructure. The misuse detection still runs.

I'm not writing this as a product recommendation, and I'd say the same thing if a different vendor shipped it first. What matters is the pattern, because the pattern is what you can now ask other vendors about.

For years the answer to "where does our data go" was some version of "to us, but we're careful." That was often true and it was never satisfying, especially in our corner of the business. Benefits data isn't ordinary corporate data. It's health conditions, salaries, dependents, leave reasons, and it's governed by HIPAA, ERISA and a stack of state laws that don't care how good the demo was.

So when a benefits team hesitates on an AI tool, that hesitation is usually correct. It isn't technophobia. It's an accurate read on what happens if this goes wrong.

What changes now is that "our data never leaves our environment" has moved from a thing vendors couldn't really offer to a thing some of them can. Which means it's fair to ask.

A few questions worth bringing to your next vendor conversation. Is our data retained after the session, and for how long? Does anything run on infrastructure we control? Who at your company can read our inputs, and under what circumstances? If you detect misuse, how did you detect it without keeping our data?

That last one is the good one. It separates vendors who have thought about this from vendors who have a privacy page.

None of this makes the diligence unnecessary. It makes it answerable, which is better than where we were.

What's stopped an AI tool from getting approved on your team, the privacy answer or something else entirely?

posts.title: Your Employees Don't Trust the AI You Just Bought
posts.excerpt: Employers are racing to add AI to their benefits stack. Employees are pumping the brakes. Here's why the gap exists—and what to do about it.
posts.body:
Sixty-seven percent of employers want to use AI to help workers make better benefits decisions. Only 28% of workers would actually trust what it tells them.

That's not a technology problem. That's a design problem.

Forrester calls it the "employer-first, employee-lagging" pattern. Employers buy AI to cut call center volume and speed up enrollment but workers want something that feels personal and has a human backstop. Both things can be true but right now, most deployments are built for the first group and handed to the second.

Here's where to start closing that gap.

First, look at what your AI tool actually says to employees. Not the pitch deck version...The real output a worker sees when they ask about their deductible or whether they should pick the HDHP. Is the recommendation just an answer, or does it show its work? Benefitfocus found that employees who received a clear rationale for AI-generated suggestions were twice as likely to act on them. Accuracy isn't enough and people need to understand why.

Second, take the privacy concern seriously instead of dismissing it. Fifty-eight percent of employees worry about data privacy when using AI-assisted benefits platforms, according to MetLife's 2024 Benefit Trends Study. That's not irrational fear. These are people sharing health status, dependent information, financial decisions. If your rollout materials don't address what data is used, how it's stored and who can see it, you've left a real question unanswered.

Third, keep humans in the picture. The 28% trust figure doesn't mean workers hate AI, it means they don't want AI instead of a person. Position the tool as a first stop, not a final answer and make it easy to escalate. "Talk to a benefits advisor" should be one click away, not buried in a footer.

Fourth, pilot with a group that will give you honest feedback...Not your most tech-comfortable employees and not HR. Find the people who usually call the benefits line with questions and watch how they interact with the tool. What confuses them? What do they skip? That's your real UX data.

Fifth, close the loop after open enrollment. Did employees who used the AI tool make different elections? Did they call in less? Did anyone complain that the recommendation felt wrong? You need that feedback to know whether the tool is actually helping or just running in the background while everyone ignores it.

My shovel metaphor holds strong here. AI can do a lot of the heavy lifting in benefits support, but only if it's built for the person swinging it...not just the person who bought it.

The employers who get this right won't just reduce call volume. They'll actually help people make better decisions about their health coverage. That's the whole point.

If your benefits AI is live but adoption is flat, it's worth asking: do your employees understand what it's telling them, and do they believe it has their interests in mind?

posts.title: What Your Employees Know About Your AI Rollout That Leadership Doesn't
posts.excerpt: The metrics look great. But there's a conversation happening on the floor that never makes it to the boardroom — and in benefits, that gap has real consequences.
posts.body:
The dashboard says adoption is up. Ticket volume is down. The board is pleased, but your entry level benefits coordinator is quietly fixing the same AI-generated enrollment error for the third week in a row.

This is the gap that doesn't show up in implementation reports.

MIT Sloan researchers have a name for it: Invisible Labor. Employees spend meaningful time correcting AI mistakes, cleaning up outputs, double-checking summaries and re-explaining things the chatbot got wrong. The productivity metrics executives track still look good, but the work behind those metrics looks different.

In benefits, this matters more than in most functions. A wrong answer about a deductible or a misread EOB isn't just an inconvenience...It's a trust problem. And the person absorbing that trust problem is usually a benefits admin who never asked for the job.

A 2024 Salesforce survey found 53% of workers are worried AI will replace their jobs and only 28% of executives rank that anxiety as a top concern. That's a 25-point gap in perception and it rarely surfaces in board reporting. Leadership isn't ignoring it out of malice, they're just not hearing it.

Gartner found that only 38% of organizations have formal mechanisms for employees to report AI-related workflow problems. The rest are making expansion decisions based on data filtered through optimistic middle-management reporting. That's not a technology problem, that's a listening problem.

The cognitive load piece compounds this. A 2023 BCG study found employees at companies with aggressive AI adoption reported 30% higher cognitive overload scores than peers at slower-adopting firms. The culprit wasn't the AI itself, it was the workflow handoffs...the moments where the human had to pick up where the tool left off, without any real re-design of how that handoff should work.

Benefits teams already carry a lot...Open enrollment pressure, employee anxiety, and compliance deadlines just to name a few. Layering a half-designed AI workflow on top of that isn't efficiency, it's just a different kind of burden.

None of this means AI doesn't belong in benefits operations. It does. But the way it gets deployed often skips the people closest to the work. The ones who know where the edge cases live, especially the ones who can tell you exactly which questions the chatbot gets wrong and why.

The right tool for hard work still requires the person doing the work to help shape how it's used.

So here's a place to start this week: ask one person on your benefits team what they're actually doing after the AI produces an output. Not whether they're using the tool. What they do next.

You might hear something the board hasn't.

posts.title: 92% of Companies Are Betting on AI. Only 1% Know What They're Doing.
posts.excerpt: McKinsey's 2025 workplace AI report lands with a number that should stop every HR leader mid-scroll: nearly every company is increasing AI investment, but almost none have figured out how to make it work at scale.
posts.body:
Nearly every company is doubling down on AI. Almost none of them are ready for it.

McKinsey's 2025 AI in the Workplace report puts the gap in plain terms: 92% of organizations plan to increase AI investment over the next three years. Only 1% describe themselves as mature in how they deploy it. That's not a technology problem. That's an execution problem.

The productivity numbers are real, but they come with a catch. Employees using AI tools on specific tasks like drafting documents, pulling data and writing code are reporting 20–30% efficiency gains. That's meaningful. The problem is those gains rarely show up in firm-wide output without deliberate workflow redesign. Individual wins don't automatically become organizational wins. Someone still has to do the plumbing.

For HR and benefits teams, this matters more than most departments want to admit. A lot of the work that buries admins...summarizing plan documents, answering routine enrollment questions, scheduling and basic analysis falls squarely in what McKinsey estimates as 60–70% of employee time currently spent on tasks generative AI can handle. That's not a threat. That's a description of work that shouldn't take this long.

But here's where the report gets honest in a way that a lot of AI vendors won't be: 65% of organizations have piloted AI. Fewer than 25% have scaled past the pilot stage. McKinsey calls this the capability trap. You run a proof of concept, it works well enough, and then it stalls because you don't have the internal talent to build on it, because people weren't brought along on the change or because no one can clearly measure what success looks like.

Benefits administration is a regulated, high-trust environment. Skepticism about AI here isn't paranoia and it's appropriate. Errors in this space have real consequences for real people. The capability trap is especially dangerous when teams feel pressure to adopt tools quickly without thinking through what happens when the tool gets something wrong.

The practical read for HR and benefits professionals: the question isn't whether to use AI. The question is whether your organization is doing the unsexy work, defining the right use cases, redesigning the workflows, measuring the right things that actually makes AI useful rather than just present.

Most companies are buying shovels and leaving them in the shed.

The 1% who describe themselves as mature aren't smarter. They just started doing the unglamorous work earlier. It's worth asking what that work looks like for your team specifically and whether the tools you're being handed were actually built for the job you're trying to do.

posts.title: The Real Reason AI Stalls in Healthcare Has Nothing to Do with the Technology
posts.excerpt: Everyone assumes AI adoption in healthcare slows down because the tools aren't good enough yet. Twenty-five years in benefits tells a different story.
posts.body:
Everyone assumes AI adoption in healthcare slows down because the tools aren't good enough yet. Fix the accuracy. Improve the interface. Add more training data. Then people will trust it.

That's not what the evidence shows.

A 2023 Nature Medicine study found that even when AI diagnostic tools outperformed clinicians in accuracy, adoption rates stayed low. Researchers gave it a name: algorithm aversion. See one AI mistake, and the distrust sticks, even if the human error rate is higher. That's not a technology problem. That's a psychology problem.

And it runs in both directions. The WHO flagged this in 2021, what they called automation bias. Some clinicians over-trust AI outputs and stop questioning them. Others reject AI reflexively. Neither response is driven by evidence. Both are driven by how we're wired.

A 2023 Wolters Kluwer survey put numbers to the skepticism. Sixty-one percent of physicians worried AI would make clinical errors. Only 38% felt confident they could even interpret AI-generated recommendations. That's not a training gap you close with a product demo. That's a trust gap built over decades of how medicine has taught people to think about authority and error.

Here's the part worth sitting with: the barrier isn't confidence in AI. It's confidence in themselves while using AI.

NEJM Catalyst found something useful here. Patient willingness to accept AI-assisted diagnoses jumped from 38% to 62% when a human clinician was described as overseeing the AI. Same tool. Same output. Different framing. The technology didn't change. The story around it did.

That should matter to everyone working in HR and benefits, not just health systems. We're in the same trust landscape. The people we serve...employees, plan members, HR admins are skeptical of automated tools for the same reasons clinicians are. They've seen a chatbot give bad information. They've watched a system fail a colleague. One bad experience overwrites a hundred good ones.

So the question isn't how do we build better AI. The question is how do we build better context around AI.

That means being honest about what the tool does and doesn't do. It means keeping a human in the loop, not as a disclaimer, but as a real part of the design. It means treating transparency as a feature, not an afterthought.

My shovel analogy holds true here. A good shovel doesn't replace the person digging. It just means the work that shouldn't take this long, doesn't. But if the person holding the shovel doesn't trust it, doesn't understand it, or got hit with it once...they're going to use their hands instead.

That's where most AI adoption efforts get stuck. Not in the algorithm. In the room where the person decides whether to pick up the tool at all.

What's your experience been, when skepticism about AI tools comes up with your team or your employees, what's actually underneath it?

posts.title: You're Spending Thousands Per Employee on Education Benefits. Do You Know If It's Working?
posts.excerpt: U.S. employers collectively spend $28 billion a year on tuition assistance. Most have no idea what they're getting for it.
posts.body:
Here's the question most benefits teams never get asked: what actually happened to the employees who used your tuition benefit last year?

Not whether they submitted receipts. Not whether the vendor processed the reimbursement. What happened to them? Did they finish the degree, did they stay, did the work get better?

For most companies, nobody knows.

A Lumina Foundation study found fewer than 25% of employers systematically track whether employees complete degrees or how education affects performance. This, despite U.S. employers spending roughly $28 billion a year on tuition assistance programs. That's not a rounding error. That's a significant line item with almost no feedback loop attached to it.

The Cigna retention finding gets cited constantly in this space, employees using tuition benefits had 8x lower turnover than non-participants. It's a striking number. But the reason it keeps getting cited is that it's unusual. Most companies never ran that analysis. Cigna did the work. Almost everyone else is just guessing.

The root cause isn't laziness. It's structure. Tuition reimbursement often lives in finance, or gets handed off to a third-party vendor, completely separate from the systems where HR tracks performance and retention. There's no natural junction where the data meets. Linkage analysis isn't just hard...it's architecturally blocked.

So benefits teams end up knowing that money went out the door, but not much else.

The participation picture is equally murky. EdAssist surveys consistently show only 2% to 5% of eligible employees actually use tuition benefits in a given year. That's a very low number for a benefit companies spend real money to offer. And most employers can't explain it. They don't know if the process is too complicated, if employees don't know the benefit exists, or if the eligible population just isn't interested.

You can't fix what you can't see.

This is exactly the kind of problem that shouldn't require a data science team to solve. The data exists...in reimbursement records, in HRIS systems, in performance reviews. The gap is that nobody has connected it and nobody has built a simple way to ask the questions.

For a benefits or HR admin, the practical starting point is small. Pull last year's tuition reimbursement list. Cross-reference it against your retention data. See if the people who used the benefit are still with the company. That one query won't give you a Cigna-level study, but it'll tell you more than you knew yesterday.

From there, the question becomes whether your systems can even support that kind of look-back and if not, that's worth surfacing. Because right now, a lot of organizations are essentially writing checks into the dark.

Twenty-eight billion dollars is a lot of shovels to hand out without ever checking whether anyone dug anything.

posts.title: The Science Behind AI-Personalized Benefits: What the Research Actually Shows
posts.excerpt: Marsh is making the case that AI can move benefits from one-size-fits-all to genuinely tailored. The data backing that claim is worth a closer look.
posts.body:
Most employees pick their benefits the same way they pick a streaming show...scroll a little, get overwhelmed, default to what they had last year.

That's not a character flaw. It's a design problem. And it's one that AI is starting to solve in ways that are measurable, not just theoretical.

Marsh recently published a piece on using AI to enhance benefits insights, focusing on the science behind personalization. The core argument: when employees get recommendations built around their actual situation, demographics, claims history, life stage, they make better decisions. Better for them, and better for the organizations paying the bills.

The numbers support that argument. A Deloitte study found that 80% of employees who received personalized benefits recommendations reported higher satisfaction. Companies using AI-driven benefits platforms saw up to a 13% reduction in healthcare costs through better plan matching. That second number matters. It's not about cutting benefits. It's about helping people choose the right ones.

Here's the part that should get any benefits professional's attention. Only 34% of employees fully understand their benefits package, according to SHRM data. That's not a new problem — we've known this for years. What's new is that organizations deploying AI-powered decision-support tools are seeing comprehension scores improve by up to 40%. Higher comprehension connects directly to better voluntary benefits participation and fewer mid-year coverage gaps. The tool does the work that a one-hour enrollment meeting never could.

The machine learning piece is worth understanding, not just accepting. Models trained on claims data, demographics and behavioral patterns can predict individual benefits utilization with 85–90% accuracy, per McKinsey Health Institute research. That means the system isn't guessing. It's identifying likely needs before open enrollment closes...proactively, not reactively.

There's also a behavioral economics angle here. Thaler and Sunstein's nudge theory is genuinely embedded in how good AI personalization engines work. When employees see a short list of tailored, simplified options instead of a full catalog, they're three times more likely to select the plan that actually fits them. The architecture of the choice matters as much as the content of the choices.

For benefits administrators, this reframes the job slightly. You're not just building a plan portfolio. You're building a decision environment. AI helps you make that environment work for the person sitting in front of the screen at 9pm trying to figure out whether they need the HSA-eligible plan.

The direction is clear. The tools exist to close the comprehension gap, improve plan selection and reduce unnecessary cost, not by restricting access, but by matching people to what they actually need.

The shovel has been here. The question is whether benefits teams are ready to pick it up.

What's the biggest barrier you're seeing to AI adoption in your benefits process...the technology, the data, or getting leadership to prioritize it?

posts.title: The benefits admin work nobody wants to do is exactly what AI is good at
posts.excerpt: The repetitive parts of benefits administration aren't going away. But they no longer have to eat your week.
posts.body:
Every benefits team I've worked with has the same pile. The renewal spreadsheet rebuilt from scratch every year. The same fifteen enrollment questions answered over and over. The stewardship report that takes three days to assemble and gets skimmed in five minutes.

None of that work is hard. That's the frustrating part. It's just slow, repetitive, and relentless.

This is the exact shape of work that AI handles well. Not the judgment calls. Not the carrier negotiation. Not the conversation with an employee who just got a scary diagnosis. The pattern work underneath all of it.

A few examples from the last year of building tools for this:

Open enrollment questions. The top twenty questions are the same at almost every employer. A well-scoped assistant trained on your plan documents can answer them accurately, around the clock, and hand the genuinely complex ones to a human.

Stewardship reporting. Pulling claims data, formatting it, writing the narrative summary. The data still has to be right and a human still has to sign off, but the assembly is automatable.

Document lookups. "Is this covered?" "What's my deductible?" "When is the COBRA deadline?" These don't require a person. They require fast, accurate access to a document.

The point isn't to remove people from benefits. It's to stop spending their time on the work that never needed a person in the first place.

Start with one task. The one you dread most this quarter. That's usually the one worth automating first.

posts.title: HR isn't slow to adopt AI because it's behind. It's slow because the stakes are real.
posts.excerpt: The skepticism in benefits and HR is rational. The answer isn't more hype. It's proof.
posts.body:
There's a story floating around that HR is behind on AI. That benefits teams are dragging their feet while the rest of the world moves on.

I don't buy it.

HR and benefits sit on top of the most sensitive data in a company. Health conditions. Salaries. Leave reasons. Protected information governed by HIPAA, ERISA, and a stack of state laws. When a marketing team's AI experiment goes wrong, someone gets a weird email. When a benefits team's AI experiment goes wrong, someone's medical information leaks.

So the caution is rational. The skepticism is earned. And the answer to it is not louder hype.

The answer is proof. Narrow, demonstrable, low-stakes proof.

Don't start by putting AI between an employee and their health plan. Start with the internal work. The report nobody likes building. The first draft of a benefits guide. The follow-up email sequence after open enrollment. Things where a mistake is a typo, not a breach.

Show the team it works on the safe stuff. Build trust the way you build it anywhere, by being right, repeatedly, when the cost of being wrong is low.

Then, and only then, you've earned the right to move closer to the sensitive work.

The industry isn't slow. It's careful. There's a difference, and the people building tools for this space would do well to respect it.
